paragraphs.title: God’s Authority and Peace in the Heights

easy.explanation: Job 25:1 says, “Then answered Bildad the Shuhite.”
easy.q: Who answered at the beginning of the passage?

easy.explanation: Verse 2 says, “he maketh peace in his high places.”
easy.q: What does God make in His high places?

easy.explanation: The verse begins, “Dominion and fear are with him.”
easy.q: What is said to be with God?

medium.explanation: The verse presents God’s dominion as accompanied by fear or reverence.
medium.q: What connection does the verse make between dominion and fear?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to exalted or heavenly realms.
medium.q: What does “high places” mean in this context?

medium.explanation: God has dominion and makes peace in the high places.
medium.q: Which pair summarizes God’s actions in the verse?

answers: He possesses authority and brings harmony
He has no power in heaven
challenge.explanation: The verse joins awe-inspiring authority with the ability to make peace.
challenge.q: What does the combination of fear and peace suggest about God?

challenge.explanation: Bildad begins by describing God’s dominion, fear, and peace-making power.
challenge.q: What is the main focus of Bildad’s words in these verses?

answers: It shows that He orders even the heavenly realm
It proves that humans control Him
It shows that He lacks power
challenge.explanation: God’s ability to make peace in the heights displays His rule over that realm.
challenge.q: Why does making peace in the high places strengthen the picture of God’s authority?

paragraphs.title: God’s Unlimited Host and Unavoidable Light

answers: Is there any number to them?
easy.explanation: The verse asks, “Is there any number of his armies?”
easy.q: What question is asked about God’s armies?

easy.explanation: The verse asks, “upon whom doth not his light arise?” implying that it arises upon everyone.
easy.q: Upon whom does God’s light not arise?

easy.explanation: The question suggests that God’s armies cannot be counted.
easy.q: What is presented as beyond numbering?

medium.explanation: The countless armies and universal light both point to God’s greatness.
medium.q: What connection does the verse make between God’s armies and His light?

medium.explanation: The word refers to organized hosts or forces belonging to God.
medium.q: What does “armies” mean in this verse?

answers: People can easily hide from it
No one can hide from it
medium.explanation: If God’s light reaches everyone, no person can escape its reach.
medium.q: What conclusion follows from the fact that God’s light arises upon everyone?

answers: A host too numerous to count
challenge.explanation: The rhetorical question emphasizes the immeasurable size of God’s host.
challenge.q: What does the question “Is there any number of his armies?” emphasize?

challenge.explanation: The verse portrays God’s light as reaching all people.
challenge.q: How is the light related to the idea that no one can hide?

challenge.explanation: The countless host and universal light both represent God’s unlimited reach and power.
challenge.q: What idea do the armies and the light share?

easy.explanation: Verse 4 asks, “How then can man be justified with God?”
easy.q: With whom is man asked whether he can be justified?

easy.explanation: The verse asks how one “that is born of a woman” can be clean.
easy.q: Who is mentioned as unable to be clean?

easy.explanation: The verse stresses humanity’s inability to stand as perfectly justified before God.
easy.q: What is the main subject of the verse?

medium.explanation: To be justified means to be regarded as righteous or innocent before God.
medium.q: What does “justified with God” mean in this context?

medium.explanation: Here, “clean” refers to moral purity or innocence.
medium.q: What does “clean” mean in this verse?

answers: One refers to an angel and one to a star
medium.q: What is the relationship between “man” and “one that is born of a woman”?

answers: To emphasize humanity’s inability to stand before God as righteous
challenge.explanation: The paired questions rhetorically stress human inability to be fully justified or clean before God.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of the two questions in the verse?

answers: Humans are limited before God’s judgment
challenge.explanation: The verse places human beings in a humble and limited position before God.
challenge.q: What relationship between humanity and divine judgment is presented?

answers: It identifies a person as an ordinary mortal
It presents a person as divine
It describes the strength of an army
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes ordinary human birth and mortality.
challenge.q: Why does the phrase “born of a woman” reinforce human limitation?

paragraphs.title: The Light of the Luminaries and Human Smallness

easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, “even to the moon, and it shineth not.”
easy.q: What does not shine, according to the passage?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “the stars are not pure in his sight.”
easy.q: Who is not pure in God’s sight?

easy.explanation: Verse 6 compares man and the son of man to a worm.
easy.q: How is man described at the end of the passage?

answers: Their light is inferior in comparison with His
They are stronger than God’s light
medium.explanation: Even the heavenly lights are presented as lacking purity and brightness before God.
medium.q: What does the comparison of the moon and stars with God’s light teach?

medium.explanation: The phrase directly means that the moon does not shine in comparison with God’s glory.
medium.q: What does “it shineth not” mean in context?

answers: Man, then the stars, then the moon
The moon and stars, then man
Man, then God, then the armies
medium.explanation: The passage first mentions the moon and stars and then applies the comparison to man.
medium.q: What is the order of comparison in these verses?

answers: If even the heavenly lights are imperfect, man is even less able to claim purity
Man is greater than the heavenly lights
Man has no connection with the comparison
challenge.explanation: The phrase creates an argument from greater to lesser: if the stars are not pure, man is even less so.
challenge.q: What does “How much less” imply when the passage turns to man?

answers: The smallness of the luminaries and man before God
challenge.explanation: Both verses portray the moon, stars, and humanity as insignificant before God.
The worm image presents human beings as extremely small and humble before God.
challenge.q: What does the repeated image of a worm emphasize?
